newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Focus on bismuth, rhodium higher.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Focus on bismuth, rhodium higher.

text.p: Lack of nearby material and brisk trader covering saw bismuth climb to straddle the psychological level of $4.00 a pound during the past week, a move that could leave the way open for an attack on $4.50 and possibly $5.00 near-term, traders said on Thursday.
Elsewhere, investment funds hoping to cash in on a buying frenzy in palladium and platinum moved rhodium to levels of around $300.00 an ounce.

Bismuth traders asked by Reuters agreed that the price for the environmentally-friendly metal has the potential to move higher, though several believed that a period of consolidation at around $4.00 may be needed.
"It's had a good run up and is in need of a breather...nothing heads up in a straight line for ever," one commented.
Since late March/early April bismuth has risen steadily from around $2.85 to current levels as market operators eyed supply/demand figures.
Major producers Mexico and Peru are said to be sold out of material, while China, running low stocks, seem unprepared to sell metal into a rising market.
Traders said that apart from China there is no available stock, while the use of bismuth in the domestic market has grown.
Chinese stocks are believed to be at historically low levels of around 100 tonnes. China produces around 1,400 tonnes a year and exports around 65 percent, traders said.

A lack of available supplies saw palladium fix at $235.00 an ounce on Thursday its highest setting since the twice-daily fix began in 1989 and its highest spot price since early 1980. The afternoon platinum fix saw prices charge to $442.00, the firmest since July 1995.
"Rhodium is having a knee-jerk reaction to the gains in palladium and platinum, though I doubt prices will move much further," one trader said.
The traders said once the investment fund buying had run its course prices would fall back as overall the market remains in good supply.
Others remained wary to any retracement in any of the group metals as platinum and palladium market-makers met in London on Thursday afternoon to discuss surging prices.
"Until palladium and platinum calm down and show some signs of easing it is unlikely that rhodium will fall back," one trader said.

Some downward pressure was seen on Russian cobalt as traders priced in metal, while opinions on high grade were divided. Several suggested that supply problems from the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia were helping to underpin the market.
Last week a senior Gecamines official told Reuters by phone from Lubumashi that the company was airfreighting material into Europe.
Several traders showed surprise as they believed that, although Gecamines was arranging for airfreight, no material so far has been moved.
One source with strong contacts in the region said, "The process of moving metal from a country recovering from seven months of civil war is not easy."

European concerns are trying to arrange a string of licences to move the metal so far they have not been forthcoming, the source said. "As far as I know licences for the movement of aircraft in and out of Lubumashi have not been granted," the source said.

Growing domestic demand in China and a lack of offers from the region underpinned molybdenum. Traders said supply and demand for molybdenum remained in balance which was leaving little material available to the spot market. - - London Newsroom +44 171 542 8075
